Position Paper: Parking Policy in a Mid-Sized City

Part 1: Parking Minimums
Position: I believe the city should repeal the parking minimums in its zoning code for every lot within half a mile of a frequent bus line. The rule makes each new apartment, shop, and clinic build a fixed number of spaces whether or not anyone will use them, and the cost lands on tenants and customers who may not own a car at all.

Part 2: Curb Pricing
Position: I believe curb space downtown should be priced by demand, with meters that rise on busy blocks and fall on empty ones until about one space on each block stays open. The revenue should stay on the blocks that produce it and pay for sidewalks, lighting, and street trees there.

Part 3: Meter Revenue
Position: I believe meter revenue should be dedicated money for the districts where it is collected, with a public report each year showing how it was spent. Whether it goes first to bus service or to sidewalk repair is a question I hold more loosely, because the council has not yet published its draft budget.

Discussion
The most contested question is whether repeal would flood nearby streets with parked cars, and I'm convinced it would not. Some critics argue that developers will build no parking at all once the rule is gone, but lenders still ask for spaces wherever the market wants them, and the cities that repealed first saw builders keep most of their garages. Our own 2015 waiver applied only to lots near routes that ran every fifteen minutes or better. Downtown lots rebuilt under that waiver now hold housing instead of required asphalt, evidence of how much space the old rule wasted.
I'm just as confident that curb pricing has to come with repeal rather than after it. Many people believe that free parking is a public service the city owes its residents, yet a free space on a crowded block is rationed by circling, which costs drivers time and fills the street with traffic that is not going anywhere. When the price is right, a driver can find a space near the door and the block still has room for deliveries. So I can support both changes at once without worrying that one of them will undo the other.
My view on the revenue question is more provisional, since the evidence from smaller cities is mixed and the budget numbers are still being drafted. I firmly believe that meter money should not be swept into the general fund, but the choice between buses and sidewalks depends on figures the city has not released. A city our size could also meter one district first and publish what it brings in before deciding. If the council asks residents to give up free parking, I want to be able to show them exactly where the money goes.
My settled view is that parking policy is a land-use question more than a traffic question. Every space a building is required to provide is a space that cannot hold an apartment, a storefront, or a tree, and the people who pay for it are often the ones who drive the least. As a future planner, I need to remember that the rules on the books shape who can afford to live near the jobs.
